title: Two canons
hookLine: the Kangyur, the Buddha's words, and the Tengyur, the commentaries

cards: Long wooden shelves in a Tibetan temple, row after row of long narrow books wrapped in cloth, each pressed between two boards. They're loose pages, wider than they are tall, stacked and tied.
Many of those pages passed through the hands of translators like yesterday's. Read the labels, and the shelves fall into two great collections.

teach.b: First, the Kangyur, usually explained as the translated word: the teachings Tibetans hold to be the Buddha's own, his sutras, his rules for monks and nuns, and the tantras, all turned from Indian languages into Tibetan.
This is the teacher's own voice, as Tibetans receive it.

Then the Tengyur, usually explained as the translated treatises: the great Indian teachers explaining, arguing, organizing, and teaching how to practice what the Buddha said. Nagarjuna on emptiness is here.
Shantideva's guide to the bodhisattva's way of life is here. So are logic, medicine, grammar and poetry, because Indian scholars studied all of them.
Why keep them apart? It's a kind of honesty. A reader always knows whether they're hearing the Buddha, as tradition receives him, or a later teacher doing their best to explain.
The commentaries are honored, studied and memorized. They just stand on a different shelf. That's a habit worth borrowing.
Much of what we hear arrives already mixed: what someone said, and what somebody else says it means. A headline, a quote passed around, a family story.
Keep the words and the commentary on separate shelves, and know which one you're holding. And look back at the week. Padmasambhava tamed the obstacles.
Samye was built as a mandala. A debate weighed gradual and sudden.
Then the dark years, Atisha's renewal, and the translator carrying the words. Today, those words find their shelves.

how: Tibetan monasteries keep the Kangyur and the Tengyur on their shelves, and in some communities the Kangyur is carried in procession or read aloud in full as an act of devotion; the Tengyur's commentaries are the core of monastic study.

games.q: you're building a Tibetan library. you have the Buddha's sutras and the great teachers' explanations. how do you shelve them?
o: mix them by topic so they read together.
keep two collections: words and commentaries.
games.why: Tibetans kept two canons, the Kangyur and the Tengyur, so a reader always knows whose voice they're hearing.

practice: On an out-breath, say silently: Kangyur, the Buddha's words; on the next, Tengyur, the commentaries, back and forth until the two names sit easily.
Then let the names rest, and simply listen to the room and the breath, to whatever is here before anyone explains it.
